text.p: The Williams team could not hide their disappointment on Sunday when the retirement of both their cars in the German Grand Prix saw them slip further behind in the drivers' and constructors' world championships.

Williams had gone into the event, the 10th round of this year's championship, with Jacques Villeneuve four points behind Michael Schumacher in the drivers' title chase and their own team three points behind Ferrari in the constructors'.

But Schumacher's second place finish behind Austrian Gerhard Berger and the retirement of both Heinz-Harald Frentzen and Villeneuve left them 10 points adrift in the drivers' championship and nine points behind in the constructors'.
When asked about the result, team chief Frank Williams simply responded: "Don't bore me", before refusing to answer further questions.

Frentzen claimed he was the innocent victim in his collision with Eddie Irvine at the opening corner, which punctured his front right tyre and forced both drivers out of the race, while Villeneuve felt slightly more aggrieved about his incident with Italian Jarno Trulli on the 34th lap.

The Canadian had run wide at the first corner, allowing Prost driver Trulli to overtake him on the run to the Clark Curve. Under-braking, Trulli then forced Villeneuve wide and he locked his brakes and spun off.
Villeneuve felt it was necessary to have a quiet word with Trulli in the Prost motor home after the race, although he did take some blame for the incident.

"Trulli got close to me, so I stayed on the inside down the straight but then he got me on the outside and pushed me too close to the grass," explained Villeneuve. "I was about to run out of road so I had to lift and got behind him.
"Then he was following me in his mirrors, left, right, left, right and when we got into the braking I was too much on the inside and locked the wheels."
Williams' third double retirement of the season certainly comes at a bad time as they bid to resurrect their title challenge following disappointing form in recent races.

The world championship now moves to circuits that are likely to suit the Ferrari, including Hungary (August 8), Belgium (August 24) and Italy (September 7), putting Williams under added pressure to make improvements if they are to have any chance of retaining their drivers' and constructors' crowns.
